title: Frankenstein

evidence.note: Verified 2026-11-22 in the full text of the Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Vol. 13, Parts 12-13 (1959), Renewal Registrations. Entry text as read: "FRANKENSTEIN, a photoplay in eight reels by Universal Pictures Corp. © 16Nov31; LP2631. Universal Pictures Co., Inc. (PWH); 120ct59; R243591." That gives original registration LP2631 (16 Nov 1931), renewal number R243591, claimant Universal Pictures Co., Inc. (PWH, work made for hire), and a renewal date printed as '120ct59' (read as 12 Oct 1959). I did not record the page number. This renewal falls in the 28th year of the term, which ran 16 Nov 1958 to 15 Nov 1959. A renewed 1931 work has a 95-year term, which runs through 31 December 2026, so the film would enter the US public domain on 1 January 2027. If no renewal had been filed in 1958 or 1959, the copyright would have ended on 31 December 1959 and the film would have entered the public domain on 1 January 1960. This entry shows a renewal was filed. Status stays undetermined only because I did not check the rest of the chain, such as the original publication and notice. Check the entry yourself in the linked volume before relying on it.
evidence.source: Catalog of Copyright Entries, Third Series, Vol. 13, Parts 12-13 (1959), Renewal Registrations (archive.org)

evidence.note: No music or score registration was examined. Whether the soundtrack was covered by the film's registration or renewal was not checked. This layer is unexamined, and any assumption that it follows the print layer is my analysis, not a sourced fact.

The film's direct source is Peggy Webling's 1927 stage play, in John L. Balderston's adaptation, which was itself based on Mary Shelley's novel. The novel dates from 1818 (revised 1831) and is long out of copyright, and the underlying story is free to adapt. The story layer rests on both the novel and the 1927 play. Universal's film-specific additions, such as the monster's visual design, are a separate matter.
evidence.source: DeWitt LLP, 'Franken-who? Copyright and spooky season's beloved character'; Wikipedia, 'Frankenstein (1931 film)'

evidence.note: Universal's monster character and franchise may support trademark claims that outlast copyright. I did not verify any specific registration.

editorial:
Universal's 1931 Frankenstein is a sought-after title for filmmakers and archivists.

The rights trap is that the film's copyright was renewed. The 1959 Catalog of Copyright Entries lists renewal R243591 by Universal Pictures Co., Inc. for the photoplay registered 16 November 1931 (LP2631). A renewed 1931 work has a 95-year term that runs through 31 December 2026, so the film would enter the US public domain on 1 January 2027. Until then, treat the film as protected. Whether the soundtrack or music has separate rights was not checked. Trademark claims on the monster were also not checked. The 1818 novel is free only as a story source, not the film's look, and I did not verify any other sources the film drew on.
faq: Can I use footage from the 1931 Universal film?

Not yet, as far as I can tell. The 1959 renewal (R243591) was found in the Catalog of Copyright Entries. The film stays protected through 31 December 2026, and the public-domain date is 1 January 2027. Music or soundtrack rights and trademark claims were not checked, so check them before using clips.
Can I adapt Mary Shelley's Frankenstein story now?

Yes, for the 1818 novel's own text and plot, which are long out of copyright. Do not copy the 1931 film's own additions, such as its distinctive visual designs, until the film itself is free. I did not verify other sources the film drew on or any trademark claims on the monster.
